clinicalPearls: Numbness of the chin and lower lip in the distribution of the mental (or inferior alveolar) nerve
It is an important red-flag sign because it is frequently caused by underlying malignancy
Recognised causes include metastatic breast and prostate cancer, lymphoma and leukaemic infiltration, and it may herald relapse
Benign causes exist (dental or local trauma, mandibular osteomyelitis, sickle cell disease), but malignancy must be excluded
The lesion may be at the mandible (mental nerve) or more proximally at the skull base or leptomeninges
Investigation targets the whole nerve pathway and a search for systemic malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Numb chin syndrome arises from injury to the mental nerve or its parent inferior alveolar/mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, anywhere from the leptomeninges and skull base to the mandibular canal and mental foramen. Malignant causes act by perineural spread, mandibular or leptomeningeal metastasis, or direct compression, which is why the sign so often reflects cancer. Benign local processes injure the nerve within the mandible. The chin and lip sensory loss reflects the terminal cutaneous territory of the affected nerve.
additionalDifferentials: Dental or mandibular local pathology / trauma
Multiple sclerosis or other trigeminal pathology
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain, skull base and mandible with attention to the trigeminal/mental nerve pathway
Investigation for systemic malignancy (imaging, tumour markers) where a cause is not evident
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis if leptomeningeal disease is suspected
Full blood count and film if leukaemia is considered
redFlags: Known or suspected malignancy (new numb chin may signal metastasis or relapse)
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is driven by the underlying cause; when due to malignancy it often signifies advanced or recurrent disease and a poor outlook, whereas benign causes may resolve.
pitfalls: Dismissing chin numbness as dental without excluding malignancy
Failing to image the entire nerve pathway including the skull base
Overlooking it as a marker of cancer relapse
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Numb chin syndrome is a red-flag sign, not a disease in itself; management targets the underlying cause rather than the numbness
Work up with imaging of the nerve pathway from skull base to mandible, MRI preferred, to look for perineural or leptomeningeal disease
Obtain a dental and mandibular assessment including an orthopantomogram to exclude benign local disease before attributing the sign to cancer
Send cerebrospinal fluid cytology when leptomeningeal involvement is suspected on imaging or clinical grounds
Pursue systemic staging with imaging, tumor markers, and blood counts when no primary is known, since breast cancer, prostate cancer, and lymphoid or leukemic infiltration are the most common causes

A new numb chin in a patient with known systemic malignancy usually signals relapse or progression and should prompt restaging and reconsideration of systemic therapy along the same lines used for that cancer's progression

For leptomeningeal or skull-base involvement, combine site-directed radiotherapy for symptomatic or bulky disease with intrathecal or systemic therapy chosen for activity against the specific tumor type, with joint oncology and neurology input
For a solid mandibular or nerve-pathway metastasis without leptomeningeal spread, local radiotherapy can be used for symptom and local control alongside systemic therapy matched to the primary tumor
Exclude and separately treat benign local causes such as dental infection, mandibular osteomyelitis, local trauma, or sickle cell vaso-occlusion, which have no role for oncologic therapy
Surgery has a mainly diagnostic role, such as biopsy of an accessible mass, rather than a definitive treatment role for the sign itself

Systemic therapy, including hormonal therapy, chemotherapy, targeted or antibody-based agents, chosen by the primary tumor's known sensitivities, is the backbone of treatment when the cause is systemic or hematologic malignancy
Neuropathic analgesia with a gabapentinoid or similar agent class can be added for symptomatic relief without altering the oncologic treatment plan
There is no dedicated line-of-therapy sequence for this sign; it follows the line-of-therapy framework of whatever malignancy is identified as the cause

Monitor with serial neurologic exam for new cranial nerve findings, repeat imaging and CSF analysis as relevant, and refer promptly to oncology, and to neurology or maxillofacial and radiation oncology as indicated, especially when initial workup does not identify a cause
